newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Ukraine likely to start new year with old budget.
newsitem.headline: Ukraine likely to start new year with old budget.

text.p: The Ukrainian parliament will vote on a draft 1997 budget on Thursday, but deputies and the government are divided about the plans and economists expect the country to muddle through early 1997 with the old budget.

The draft is one of two currently in circulation in the former Soviet republic, which was initially slow to adopt market oriented reforms and where parliament is dominated by conservatives who favour subsidies and Soviet-style handouts.
Western diplomats said it could take months to overcome the chaos, even though the constitution states a new budget must be passed by January 1.
"It's very confusing because they have multiple versions," said an economist, who suggested the earliest the country of 51 million people would have a new budget was later in January.
Parliament has already passed a resolution to carry the 1996 budget into the new year.

The government hurriedly put together the first of two versions in September but President Leonid Kuchma flatly refused to sign it, saying it failed to support the industrial sector and contained unrealistic figures.
The government did not withdraw the first version because under Ukrainian parliamentary procedure such a move would have halted the entire budgetary process.

Waiting in line is the second version presented last month by Deputy Prime Minister in charge of economic reform Viktor Pynzenyk and approved by the International Monetary Fund (IMF). It has been lauded by Western funding bodies for its proposed tough spending cuts, tax reform measures and looser investment regulations.
Pynzenyk's draft called for Ukraine's first post-Soviet economic growth of 1.7 percent compared to a forecast drop of seven percent in gross domestic product (GDP) this year.

It also called for a deficit of 5.5 percent of GDP, or four percent by Western calculations, against a 6.2 percent deficit for 1996. Annual inflation would be 25 percent, down from an expected 38 percent this year.
Diplomats said its passage could bring billions of dollars in foreign aid from Western funding bodies because of its tough reform moves.
"The only package that's acceptable to Western international financial institution (IFI) donors is comatose at the moment and will have to be revived in the first quarter of 1997," one diplomat said.
A group of international donors on Wednesday promised more than $5 billion over the next three years to Ukraine, provided it continued to implement economic reforms.
Also hinging on the second budget is a three-year, $2.5 to $3 billion Extended Fund Facility (EFF) from the IMF, to replace an $867 million standby loan.

But diplomats said the government would have to work harder to lobby parliament to pass the second draft budget, since it would prove unpopular with Ukrainians already weary after five years of difficult economic conditions.

"If it's just Pynzenyk out there twisting in the wind, that's not a recipe for success," one diplomat said. He added that once parliament eventually returned to reviewing the second version it could ask the government to make major changes to it.
